name: Lateral raise
angleNote: 0° = arm by your side, 90° = arm horizontal at shoulder height, 180° = overhead (Lu raise). Front view: x points out to the side.
jointNote: Not truly one joint: the shoulder blade turns upwards on the rib cage as the arm rises, so the angle here is the whole arm against the trunk. In 12 people reaching overhead, the shoulder joint itself moved about 2.3° for every 1° of shoulder-blade rotation on the way up (2.7 on the way down), and the first 30° came mostly from the shoulder joint (about 3.7 : 1); Inman's classic figure is 2 : 1. Above about 30° a good part of the raise is the shoulder blade turning. The model treats the arm as turning about one fixed shoulder point; the shoulder-blade muscles (trapezius, serratus anterior) that turn the blade aren't analysed.
jointNoteSource: Braman JP, Engel SC, LaPrade RF, Ludewig PM (2009). In vivo assessment of scapulohumeral rhythm during unconstrained overhead reaching in asymptomatic subjects. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 18(6):960–967. doi:10.1016/j.jse.2009.02.001

segments.massNote: Segment mass as a fraction of body mass, and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end, from de Leva's adjusted Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov table (young adult males). The forearm segment includes the hand (combined centre of mass along elbow → grip).
segments.massSource: de Leva P (1996). Adjustments to Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov's segment inertia parameters. J Biomech 29(9):1223–1230. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(95)00178-6 (Table 4, males)
segments.note: Shoulder→elbow and elbow→grip centre in metres, typical adult. The arm is modelled straight; a soft elbow shortens the lever slightly.

strengthCurve.label: Shoulder abductor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative shoulder-abduction strength vs abduction: strongest at 30°, weakest with the arm by the side (0°). From a conference abstract (hand-held myometer, 30 adults): +31.3% at 30°, +12.5% at 60° and −18.8% at 0° relative to 90°; Mayer et al. 1994 place the isometric peak at 27–65° in men. The weakest evidence of the curves here. Peak torque default: Mayer's isometric shoulder abduction, men, 47 ± 12 Nm. The sources disagree near the start: Clarke et al. (64 men, supine, via Kulig et al.) found abduction strongest with the arm by the side and a plateau at 45–90°. Treat the 0–30° part as uncertain. Above 90° (the overhead variant) the 90° value is held: no measured curve was found that goes higher (Mayer et al. place the isometric peaks in front of the body and below head level; Kulig et al. describe a clear drop in flexion strength beyond about 110°, without numbers), so effort overhead is probably underestimated.
strengthCurve.source: Haidar SG, Lloyd J, Cox D, Deshmukh S (2009). Shoulder abduction strength: is it affected by the degree of abduction? J Bone Joint Surg Br 91-B Suppl I:160 (conference abstract). doi:10.1302/0301-620X.91BSUPP_I.0910160c; Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Normal values of isokinetic maximum strength, the strength/velocity curve, and the angle at peak torque of all degrees of freedom in the shoulder. Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25. doi:10.1055/s-2007-1021105; Kulig K, Andrews JG, Hay JG (1984). Human strength curves. Exerc Sport Sci Rev 12:417–466 (Clarke et al., contrary finding at 0°)

muscles.name: Lateral deltoid
muscles.note: Main abductor once the arm is away from the side; its moment arm grows as the arm rises. wger has no separate map for the lateral head. 30% of maximum at 60% 1RM, with the rear deltoid at 24% and the front at 21% (Campos et al., thumbs forward), close to these weights' ratios.
muscles.source: Campos YAC, Vianna JM, Guimarães MP, Oliveira JLD, Hernández-Mosqueira C, da Silva SF, Marchetti PH (2020). Different shoulder exercises affect the activation of deltoid portions in resistance-trained individuals. J Hum Kinet 75:5–14. doi:10.2478/hukin-2020-0033 (13 men, 60% 1RM, % of maximal isometric activation)

placementFactor.note: Arm rotation (thumbs up / forward / down), relative to thumbs forward, from Coratella et al.'s lateral raises: front deltoid ~80 / 36 / 34%, middle ~48 / 55 / 52%, rear ~36 / 52 / 85% of maximal activation. Each variant was done at its own 8-RM, so these are relative levels, not the same load.
placementFactor.source: Coratella G, Tornatore G, Longo S, Esposito F, Cè E (2020). An electromyographic analysis of lateral raise variations and frontal raise in competitive bodybuilders. Int J Environ Res Public Health 17(17):6015. doi:10.3390/ijerph17176015 (Discussion: deltoid sEMG RMS, % of maximal isometric, 10 male bodybuilders, seated, 8-RM, raise to 90°)

muscles.name: Posterior deltoid
muscles.note: Also abducts with the arm out to the side, and takes over when the arm turns in (thumbs down). Level with the thumbs forward: about as active as the middle deltoid (Coratella et al.: 52% vs 55% of maximum); the shape over the angle follows the middle deltoid (estimate).
muscles.source: Coratella G, Tornatore G, Longo S, Esposito F, Cè E (2020). An electromyographic analysis of lateral raise variations and frontal raise in competitive bodybuilders. Int J Environ Res Public Health 17(17):6015. doi:10.3390/ijerph17176015 (Discussion: deltoid sEMG RMS, % of maximal isometric, 10 male bodybuilders, seated, 8-RM, raise to 90°)

Each variant was done at its own 8-RM, so these are relative levels, not the same load.

muscles.name: Supraspinatus
muscles.note: Helps start the raise and keeps the head of the humerus centred in the socket; relatively more important early in the range.
muscles.source: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Soderberg GL (2003). Surface electromyographic analysis of exercises for the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 33(5):247–258. doi:10.2519/jospt.2003.33.5.247 (Tables 1, 3, 4: 30 adults, loaded raises in the scapular plane, % of maximal isometric activation)

muscles.name: Anterior deltoid
muscles.note: Assists abduction, and takes over more if the arm drifts forward of the body or turns out (thumbs up). Level with the thumbs forward: about two thirds of the middle deltoid's (Coratella et al.: 36% vs 55% of maximum); the shape over the angle is an estimate.
muscles.source: Coratella G, Tornatore G, Longo S, Esposito F, Cè E (2020). An electromyographic analysis of lateral raise variations and frontal raise in competitive bodybuilders. Each variant was done at its own 8-RM, so these are relative levels, not the same load.

muscles.name: Upper trapezius
muscles.note: Rotates the shoulder blade upwards as the arm rises. Shown on the back body map. About 72% of maximum in loaded raises below 80°, 79% above 120° (Ekstrom et al.), in line with these weights.
muscles.source: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Soderberg GL (2003). Surface electromyographic analysis of exercises for the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 33(5):247–258. doi:10.2519/jospt.2003.33.5.247 (Tables 1, 3, 4: 30 adults, loaded raises in the scapular plane, % of maximal isometric activation)

muscles.name: Serratus anterior
muscles.note: Turns the shoulder blade upwards (with the trapezius) so the arm can rise out to the side and up; its share grows as the arm goes up, and most of the motion above shoulder height is the shoulder blade turning. The model has no shoulder blade; the weights follow EMG. Loaded raises in the scapular plane (Ekstrom et al.): serratus anterior 62% of maximum below 80° and 96% above 120°, lower trapezius 50% and 61%, upper trapezius 72% and 79%.
muscles.source: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Soderberg GL (2003). Surface electromyographic analysis of exercises for the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 33(5):247–258. doi:10.2519/jospt.2003.33.5.247 (Tables 1, 3, 4: 30 adults, loaded raises in the scapular plane, % of maximal isometric activation); direction from Braman JP, Engel SC, LaPrade RF, Ludewig PM (2009). In vivo assessment of scapulohumeral rhythm during unconstrained overhead reaching in asymptomatic subjects. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 18(6):960–967. doi:10.1016/j.jse.2009.02.001 (direction only)

muscles.name: Lower trapezius
muscles.note: Part of the upward-rotation pair with the serratus anterior and upper trapezius, mostly overhead. Loaded raises in the scapular plane (Ekstrom et al.): serratus anterior 62% of maximum below 80° and 96% above 120°, lower trapezius 50% and 61%, upper trapezius 72% and 79%.
muscles.source: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Soderberg GL (2003). Surface electromyographic analysis of exercises for the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 33(5):247–258. doi:10.2519/jospt.2003.33.5.247 (Tables 1, 3, 4: 30 adults, loaded raises in the scapular plane, % of maximal isometric activation); direction from Braman JP, Engel SC, LaPrade RF, Ludewig PM (2009). In vivo assessment of scapulohumeral rhythm during unconstrained overhead reaching in asymptomatic subjects. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 18(6):960–967. doi:10.1016/j.jse.2009.02.001 (direction only)

phases.name: Start
phases.text: Arm by your side. A dumbbell's line of action passes close to the shoulder, so there's little torque here. A cable from the opposite side already pulls the arm across the body.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: The free-weight moment arm grows with the sine of the angle. The deltoid's leverage improves too, and the shoulder blade starts to rotate upwards.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: Arm near horizontal. With a dumbbell the moment arm is the full arm length just as abductor strength is falling off, so this is the sticking point.

phases.name: Overhead
phases.text: Above shoulder height (Lu raise): the load's lever shrinks again, and the shoulder blade turning upwards carries more of the motion.

variants.name: Standing dumbbell lateral raise
variants.notes: Gravity pulls straight down, so torque = m·g·L·sin(angle): zero with the arm by your side and maximum at shoulder height. The bottom of the range is almost unloaded.

variants.name: Cable lateral raise (low pulley, opposite side)
variants.notes: The cable comes from a low pulley on the other side of your body, so it pulls the arm across you even at the bottom. The torque curve is much flatter than with a dumbbell. In this flat front view the cable seems to pass through the body; in reality it runs just in front of or behind it.

variants.name: Lateral raise machine

camProfiles.label: Illustrative cam
camProfiles.note: Effective radius in metres: joint torque per unit of stack weight, including any lever or pulley ratio. Illustrative shape, not measured from a specific machine.
camProfiles.source: TODO: replace with a measured profile (torque per kg at each angle) for a real machine

camProfiles.label: Round pulley (constant)
camProfiles.note: A plain round pulley: the lever between the belt and the axle never changes, so the resistance torque is the same at every angle (physics, no source needed). Many plate-loaded and budget machines work like this. Radius 0.30 m, nominal (stack kg don't compare between machines).
camProfiles.source: Physics: a round pulley's radius is constant (no source needed)

variants.notes: A pad on the upper arm near the elbow pushes against the raise, and the cam sets the resistance at each angle. This illustrative cam loads the start far more than a dumbbell and stays fairly even. Machine stack weights don't compare directly with dumbbell weights: the same number of kg gives a different torque.

variants.name: Band lateral raise (band under the foot)
variants.notes: Band anchored under the foot on the working side. Nearly slack at the bottom, so the start is easy; tension and moment arm both grow as the arm rises, making the top much harder than with a dumbbell. The load slider is the band's tension at 1.6 m (about its length at shoulder height).

variants.name: Lu raise (to overhead, thumbs up)
variants.notes: A lateral raise continued over the head, usually with the thumbs turned up (the arm rotated outwards) and light weights. The load's lever peaks at shoulder height and shrinks to zero overhead, so the hardest point is still around 90°; above it the shoulder blade does more and more of the turning (serratus anterior, trapezius). The arm-rotation setting starts at thumbs up, which shifts work to the front deltoid.

wger.name: Lateral Raises
wger.note: Checked against wger's public exercise list (id = the number in the page address).

placement.label: Arm rotation
placement.hint: Turning the arm changes which part of the deltoid lifts it, not the load: the lever and the torque stay the same. Measured in bodybuilders (Coratella et al.): thumbs up shifts the work to the front deltoid (about 80% of its maximum vs 36% with the thumbs forward), thumbs down to the rear deltoid (85% vs 52%), with the upper trapezius and triceps also working harder; the middle deltoid is about the same in all three (48–55%).

placement.label: Elbow bend
placement.hint: 0° = arm straight. A bent elbow points the forearm forward, out of the plane of the raise, so seen from the front the weight comes closer to the shoulder: the lever is upper arm + forearm × cos(bend). At 90° only the upper arm's length is left: about half the torque for the same dumbbell. The deltoid works the same way; it just needs less force.
